transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

I guess… the short version is that I can’t keep up with myself anymore. At work I’m an industrial production manager, so planning and fixing systems is literally part of my job, but recently I went way past normal.

I started launching plant redesign projects one after another, like I’d see a bottleneck on the floor and suddenly I’d be mapping out a full layout change, contacting suppliers, comparing equipment options, calling people after hours because I felt like it couldn’t wait. I was rewriting the shift plan myself, like not just editing it, but sitting there trying to rebuild the whole thing on my own because I was convinced I could make everything more efficient if I just pushed hard enough.

And then it was like… all those plans were already in motion, people were asking me for decisions, timelines, follow-ups, and suddenly I couldn’t keep up with the very things I’d started. It’s embarrassing because I’m usually very capable, and I know how production schedules work, I know how to manage projects, but this felt like I’d created a machine that started running faster than I could handle. That’s why I came in.
During this period, were you sleeping much less than usual but still feeling rested?

Yes. Very much, actually. I was sleeping maybe two or three hours a night, sometimes just sort of lying down because I knew I was supposed to, not because I felt tired in the normal way.

And the strange part is I’d still show up at the plant feeling sharp, almost too sharp. Like charged up. I remember thinking sleep was kind of optional, or inefficient, like it was this unnecessary pause when I could be using that time to think through plans or get ahead of things. At the time it didn’t feel like a problem—it felt like I’d figured out how to function on less. But looking back, two or three hours and then walking in like I was fully rested was… not normal for me.
During that time, did you feel unusually euphoric or unusually irritable?

Yes… both, honestly. At the beginning, especially when this assignment really started ramping up, I felt almost electrically upbeat. Like not just in a good mood, but like everything was bright and obvious and I could see all the connections at once. I remember walking through the plant and feeling this rush, like, “Of course, this is what needs to happen, why hasn’t anyone done this already?” It felt exciting, almost like I was plugged into something.

But then it shifted, or maybe it was happening at the same time—I got weirdly irritable. If anyone questioned one of my ideas or asked me to slow down and justify something, I took it as them getting in the way of something that was clearly important. I’d feel this flash of anger, like they were dragging their feet on purpose, even if they were probably just doing their jobs and asking normal questions. At the time it felt like they were slowing down something obvious. Looking back, my reaction was way bigger than the situation called for.
During that time, were you talking much more than usual?

Yes. Definitely. I mean, I’m usually someone who explains things thoroughly because of my job, but this was different. In meetings I could actually hear myself talking faster than usual, and I’d just keep going.

I’d start on one point, like line speeds, and before anyone could really respond I’d be moving into staffing coverage, then supplier delays, then some equipment issue, then back to the schedule. It wasn’t like a normal discussion where people ask questions and you pause and adjust. It was more like I was trying to unload everything in my head before it disappeared, and it all felt connected, so I didn’t want to stop.

I remember seeing people kind of waiting for an opening to speak, and I knew on some level that I was taking up too much space, but I also felt like if I slowed down, we’d lose momentum. So yes, I was talking much more than usual—faster, longer, and jumping between topics in a way that probably made sense to me more than to everyone else.
During that period, did your behavior become so severe that you had to be hospitalized?

I… I don’t think I was hospitalized for it, no. At least, not that I’m aware of in the way you mean—like being admitted somewhere because of how I was acting.

It got intense, and people around me were definitely concerned at points, but I didn’t end up in a hospital during that period. I’m hesitating because it’s hard to judge what counts as “severe enough,” you know? At the time I wasn’t seeing it clearly, so if you had asked me then, I probably would’ve said everything was fine or that everyone else was overreacting. But in terms of an actual hospital admission, no, I don’t have that to report.
During that time, did your behavior cause serious problems at work or in your relationships?

Yes. It did. I don’t think I fully understood how serious it was in the moment, but looking back, it definitely caused real problems at work.

There was one shift-planning meeting where I got so wound up and unable to track the actual decisions we needed to make that I had to ask to be pulled out of it. And that’s… that’s not a small thing in my role. Shift planning is basic, core production management. It’s not some extra optional meeting where I can just be intense and everyone works around me. People depend on me being able to make practical calls about staffing and timing and what needs to happen on the floor.

Occupational health ended up getting involved because I wasn’t functioning properly in that part of my job. I wasn’t able to carry out basic production decisions that my role depends on, and I think people could see that it had gone beyond me just being stressed or passionate about the work. At the time I felt embarrassed and defensive, like they were overreacting or taking control away from me, but now I can see why they were concerned.
Before this high-energy period, have you ever had a time when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day for at least two weeks?

Yes. Before that high-energy stretch, I had been in a really heavy depressed period for… about three months, I’d say. It wasn’t just a few bad days or a rough week where I could shake it off over the weekend. It was most of the day, nearly every day, and it just kept going.

The move and the new plant assignment made it much harder to manage. I think at first I tried to frame it as adjustment stress, like, “Of course I feel awful, I’m dealing with a big transition, I’m in a demanding role, everything is unfamiliar.” But it lasted long enough that it didn’t feel like just settling in anymore. It was like this weight that followed me through the day, and even when I was doing the things I had to do, it was still there.

So yes—definitely more than two weeks. Closer to three months.
